3. Facts disclosed in the petition traced his career since he joined the service of the Government of East Bengal as Assistant Surgeon in 1952 till he became the Director of the Institute in 1972. After getting several promotions since he joined service he was confirmed as Professor of Medicine on April 24, 1963, Besides performing his duties he carried on research in Medical Science and published a number of articles and also books. In 1965 the appellant was appointed the Joint Director of the Institute and in March, 1967 was appointed to act as Professor of Medicine in addition to his duties as Joint Director. 

 4. In July, 1969 the Government decided to convert the post of Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute into non-practising administrative post of Director. In July 1969 & January, 1971 the Government enquired from the appellant if he would be willing to accept the non-practising administrative post of Director of the Institute. The appellant by his letter of January 12, 1971 replied that he would accept the post of Director only if he was allowed to continue as Professor of Medicine which entitled him to the right of private practice. After the emergence of Bangladesh the idea to convert the post of Director and Professor of Medicine into a non-practising administrative post was given up by the Government and by notifications issued on January 1, 1972 and November 12, 1972 the appellant was appointed Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute with effect from 19.1.71. The Government granted the appellant ad-hoc rank and status of Joint Secretary in 1974 and in 1975 he was given the ad-hoc rank and status of Additional Secretary and during the period of 1974-1975 the appellant was the personal physician of the President of Bangladesh. 

 5. On November 22, 1978 the appellant was issued with a notice which purported to make the post of Director a non-practising post and relieve him of his duties and designation of Professor of Medicine. The legality of this notice was challenged by the appellant in Writ Petition No 571 of 1979. On December 6, 1979 this notice was declared by a Bench of this High Court Division to have been made without lawful authority. In spite of this declaration the impugned notification under sec 9(2) of the Act was issued by the Government. The appellant challenged legality of this notification on various grounds by filing a Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution alleging, inter alia, mala fide in the Government in causing his premature retirement. 

 6. Some facts which appear in the petition may seem to be relevant for deciding the legality or otherwise of the impugned notification. The appellant completed 25 years of service on 10.4.1977. Due to scarcity of doctors restriction has been imposed on government doctors in seeking employment outside the country. For the same reason as many as 34 doctors who have completed 25 years of service have not been retired. To show the malice in law it was stated that many of these doctors were senior to the appellant in service. Further, there had been no allegations against him for inefficiency, negligence or misconduct. No reason, valid or otherwise, appears from the impugned notification for his premature retirement. The appellant completed 25 years of service more than a year before the order impugned in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 was passed. It was, therefore, claimed that the impugned notification issued on June 5, 1980 was issued for achieving collateral purposes and the order contained therein amounted to compulsory retirement. 

 7. Besides stating these facts, the appellant also mentioned that no principle or guideline was provided in section 9(2) of the Act for the exercise of discretion by the Government. The absence of any principle or guideline left scope for discrimination between government servants who completed 25 years of service. The resulting discrimination, it was claimed, was violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution and power conferred Upon the Government amounted to uncontrolled discretion amounting to discrimination. It was also equivalent to the power of compulsorily retiring a government servant which is a major penalty under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976, and as such an order made under section 9(2) of the Act is a punishment and amounted to removal within the meaning of Article 135 of the Constitution. Since the appellant was not given any opportunity of being heard before the impugned notification was issued it is violating Article 135 as well. 

 9. In a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondents it was mentioned that 11 government doctors had voluntarily retired. In his supplementary affidavit-in-reply the appellant mentioned that those doctors voluntarily retired because they obtained lucrative jobs in foreign countries. 

 10. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, after hearing the parties, discharged the Rule on July 29, 1980. It was held, inter alia, that (i) the Act had apparently been made in terms of paragraph 10(2) (b) of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution and in view of Article 150 of the Constitution the Act was to have effect notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution including Part III of the Constitution ; (ii) section 9(2) of the Act was not ex facie discriminatory inasmuch as it has been made applicable to all government servants and it contains an element of mutuality ; (iii) when a law was not ex facie discriminatory, the party challenging its constitutionality must show that it had been administered in an unjust, discriminatory manner ; (iv) discretionary power was not necessarily discriminatory and abuse of discretion was not to be easily assumed where discretion, vested in the Government ; (v) a long series of decisions of superior Courts in India and Pakistan upheld the discretion of the Government to order premature retirement ; (vi) in three of its decisions they High Court Division held that section 9(2) of the Act was not ultra vires the Constitution and though the argument of violation of Articles 27 and 29 was not advanced in those cases in the manner it had been done in this case, it appeared that the Court was not unmindful about all the provisions of the Constitution; (vii) an order of compulsory retirement was not passed by way of punishment nor the order showed any stigma, and the government servant was not deprived of any vested right and, therefore, such an order could not be termed as removal ; and (viii) in the earlier case the Court rejected the allegation of mala fide and the appellant had not alleged any mala fide specifically against the present Minister who had not been impleaded. 

 12. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the appellant, challenged not only the order of retirement of the appellant from service but also provisions of law, namely, section 9(2) of the Act under which the order was made, as being violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. He submitted that section 9(2) was ex fade discriminatory inasmuch as it conferred arbitrary, uncontrolled and unguided discretion on the Government in the matter of selecting a government servant for retirement who answered the description provided therein. There was no restraint on its power to select and so to discriminate. Presumption of constitutionality, no doubt, attaches to every piece of legislation, he submitted but such presumption cannot make a law constitutional if, on examination of such law, element of discrimination was discovered in it. 

 14. Quoting the impugned order, the learned Counsel mentioned that no reason is discernible therein nor any indication whatsoever has been given in the affidavits as to why an eminent doctor like the appellant was being prematurely retired. The age of retirement for government servant, it may be mentioned here, has been fixed at 57 years under section 4 of the Act with provision for extension under certain condition, upto 60 years in the case of a physician or a teacher. The impugned order is as follows: 

 Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 (Act No. XII of 1974) the Government is pleased to direct that the said Dr. Nurul Islam shall retire from service with immediate effect.” 

 15. Referring to his ability as a reputed doctor and his academic performance which are not disputed by the respondents, the learned Counsel submitted that in such background there cannot be even any possibility for thinking that the appellant had been retired on the ground of inefficiency, negligence or misconduct in the performance of his duties. After obtaining the degree of M.B. from the University of Calcutta the appellant joined the service of the Government of East Bengal as Assistant Surgeon on April 10, 1952. He obtained T.D.D. degree from the University of Wales and M.R.C.P. degree from Edinburgh. He was appointed Professor of Medicine 1962 and was confirmed in this post in 1963. He got to his credit the publication of a number of articles and books in the field of medical sentence and in recognition thereof he was made F.R.C.P. (London). While the appellant was serving as Professor of Medicine in the Chittagong Medical College he was appointed to act as the Joint Director of the Institute. On March 31, 1967 he was appointed as Professor of Medicine in the Institute in addition to his duties as Joint Director. When in March, 1970 Sir James Cameron, the Director, who was also a Professor of Medicine of the Institute, left for the United Kingdom, the appellant was put in charge of the Office of the Director of the Institute in addition to his duties as the Joint Director and Professor of Medicine. 

 16. Though before the emergence of Bangladesh there was some thinking by the relevant Ministry concerned of changing the post of Director and Professor of Medicine into a non-practising administrative post of Director of the Institute and as early as July, 1969 enquiry was made whether the appellant would be willing to accept the post of Director of the Institute as a non-practising administrative post which, of course, he declined to accept, the Government of Bangladesh, by notifications issued on January 5, 1972 and November 24, 1972 appointed the appellant as Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute with effect from January 19, 1971. The right to continue as Professor of Medicine carried with it the right to private practice. 

 17. About a year and a half later, that is, on November 22, 1978, the appellant received Government Notification No. Per-I/IM-35/78/951 which purported to relieve the appellant of his duties and designation of Professor of Medicine of the Institute as there was no such post there. The notification also purported to make the post of the Director of the Institute a non-practising post. In this connection, reference was made to the decision of the Government of East Pakistan which has been referred to above. The appellant challenged the legality of the notification in his Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. It was claimed therein that the appellant had the right to continue as Professor of Medicine which carried with it the right to private practice. Since this was an essential condition of his service as the Director of the Institute it was guaranteed by the Constitution of Bangladesh and the Government had no power to vary the pre-existing terms and conditions of his service which are continued by paragraph 10 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution. 

 18. After hearing the appellant and the respondents who contested the appellant's Writ application, a Bench of the High Court Division set aside the impugned order after declaring it as being of no legal effect and having been made without lawful authority. Costs were awarded against the Government. 

 19. It was asserted that, on its failure to dislodge the appellant, the Government issued the impugned notification purporting to retire the appellant from service in exercise of the power conferred on it by section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974. It was surprising to note, the learned Counsel submitted, that when, in view of the extreme shortage of doctors, the Government had been discouraging the doctors for taking up employment abroad and requiring the Government doctors who wish to serve abroad to retire from the Government service and had also issued directive that no doctor below the age of 58, whether in Government service or not who wishes to go abroad, should go out of the country without obtaining prior clearance from the Ministry of Health and Population Control, the authority concerned compulsorily retired the appellant from service before he reached the age of superannuation. Moreover, there were as many as 34 government doctors who had completed 25 years of service but have not been retired from service of the Government under section 9(2) of the Act. 

 20. By quoting from a paragraph in the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the Government in the former case, namely, Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 the learned Counsel tried to show that the merit of the appellant as a doctor was undoubtedly recognized even by the Government the paragraph reads as follows: 

 21. It was submitted that from the facts and circumstances stated above it would appear that the Government had no valid reason to retire the appellant from service. It was further submitted that after the judgment in the previous Writ Petition the Government should not have adversely affected the appellant's position, by issuing the notification retiring him from service altogether. The impugned notification appears to have been issued in order to circumvent that judgment. It is, therefore, mala fide as having been issued for achieving some collateral purposes. Before proceeding further I consider it necessary to refer to the provisions of both the Constitution and a few enactments including rules made thereunder, whose effect on the validity or otherwise of the impugned order has to be determined by us. 

 "27. All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law." The next Article, that is, actually clause (1) of Article 29 of the Constitution which guarantees equal opportunity in the. Government service provides as follows: "There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic." 

 22. Though the learned Counsel for the appellant directed his efforts to establishing discriminatory treatment meted out to the appellant he, in course of his argument, also mentioned the violation of Article 135 of the Constitution which provides for giving an opportunity of being heard before any order of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank is made by the Government. Reference is, therefore, made to Article 135 of the Constitution. 

 (a) "Corporation" means anybody corporate constituted or established by or under any law and includes any other body or organization set up by the Government; 

 (b) "nationalized enterprise" includes any commercial or industrial enterprise bank, firm, tea estate or any other enterprise owned by or vested in the Government or any corporation or local authority. 

 Provided that the Government or any authority authorized by the Government in this behalf may extend the service of a public servant who is a physician or teacher beyond the date of his retirement for a period non exceeding three years and such extension shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be prescribed by rules made under this Act. 

 (2) the Government may, at any time, retire from service a public servant who has completed twenty-five years of service without assigning any reason. 

 10. Public servants not entitled to retirement benefits in certain cases.—If Government or, as the case may be, employer or any departmental proceedings are pending against a public servant at the time of his retirement or, as the case may be, ceasing to be in service, he shall not be entitled to any pension or other retirement benefits, except his subscriptions to any provident fund and the interest thereon, till the determination of such proceedings, and the payment to him of any pension or other retirement benefits shall be subject to the findings in such proceedings. 

 11. Power to make rules. The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. 

 24. Mention may be made that previous to this enactment the Government of Bangladesh had enacted a similar law which is found the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Order, 1972 (P.O. 14 of 1972). This statute was protected by the Constitution. The relevant article of this Order, namely, Article 5, which deals with the optional retirement is quoted below: 

 Provided further that public servant who is either in service on extension or re-employment on the date of promulgation of this Order against whom a department criminal proceeding initiated by the Government is pending shall be deemed to be on re-employment on the expiry or termination of his extension or re-employment during the pendency of the proceeding on such terms and conditions as the prescribed authority may determine : 

 25. The Counsel for the appellant submitted that even though this enactment containing the aforesaid provisions were protected by the Constitution, it would be seen that the rules made under this law provided the principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion in this respect by the Government. Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement Rules 1973 which were made under P.O. 14 of 1972 is as follows : 

 “3. Government may retire a public servant after he has completed 25 years qualifying service on any of the following grounds: 

 26. On the other hand, no principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government in the matter of retiring a Government servant on the completion of 25 years of service is provided in the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1975. The learned Counsel however, referred to the rules made under section 9(2) of the Act, Rule 9 is as follows: 

 27. He pointedly referred to the omission of any principle or guideline in the rules made under section 9(2) of the Act. In stressing the need for providing some principles or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government, the learned counsel submitted that even under the Civil Service Regulations, Fundamental Rules, the East Pakistan Service Rules and Article 178 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962 such guidelines were provided. Provisions in the Civil Service Regulations are as follows:— 

 (2)	A retiring pension is also granted to an officer who is required by Government to retire after completing twenty five years qualifying service or more. 

 Note 1.—Government retains an absolute right to retire any officer after he has completed 25 years, qualifying service without giving any reasons, and no claim to special compensation on this account will be entertained. This right will not be exercised except when it is in the public interest to dispense with the further services of an officer. 

 (2) A retiring pension is also granted to an officer who is required by Government to retire after completing 25 years' qualifying service or more. Note 1-Government retains an absolute right to retire any officer after he has completed twenty-five yews' qualifying service without giving any reasons and no claim to special compensation on this account will be entertained. This right will not be exercised except when it is in the public interest to dispense with the further service of the officer." 

 "F.R. 55(a) Except as otherwise provided in the other clauses of this rule, the date of compulsory retirement of a Government servant, other than a ministerial servant, is the date on which he attains the age of 55 years. He may be retained in service after the date of compulsory retirement with the sanction of the local Government on public grounds which must .be recorded in writing, but he must not be retained after the age of 60 years except in very special circumstances." 

 (2) A retiring pension is also granted to an officer who is required by Government to retire after completing twenty-five years qualifying service or more. 

 Note 1.—Government retains an absolute right to retire any officer after he has completed twenty-five years' qualifying service without giving any reasons and no claim to special compensation of this account will be entertained. This right will not be exercised except when it is in the public interest to dispense with the further service of an officer." 

 28. In support of his contention that section 9(2) of the Act is ex facie discriminatory, the learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that nowhere in the Act any principle or guideline has been laid down to regulate the exercise of power by the Government to, retire a government servant who completed 25 years of service. He took us through the preamble of the Act and provisions of sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10 of the Act. Provisions of none of these sections give any indication whatsoever as to how the government would make selection, from among the government servants who have completed 25 years, a particular government servant for retirement before he has attained the age of superannuation namely, 57 years. There should be some criteria or yardstick in the Act itself which has conferred such discretion. Such criteria or yardstick may not have been necessary if there was no question of selection of some from the many involved in the group, from which the selection has to be made. Section 9(2) clearly indicates that there is a need for classification whenever the power conferred on the Government has to be exercised in relation to a group of officers similarly situated. The learned Counsel mentioned that instead of providing any principle or guideline either in the Act or the rule the legislature has left scope for the Government to make such selection arbitrarily. As a result, not only in the impugned notification but also in the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondents no reason has been given as to why the appellant had been selected for premature retirement out of so many doctors answering the description mentioned in section 9(2) of the Act, It seems that for this reason the respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition stated that the appellant was retired from service in accordance with law. No other fact has been disclosed in the affidavit-in-opposition indicating the ground for which the appellant had been retired He further mentioned that there is no co-relation between sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of the Act Sub-section (1) gives an opportunity to Government servants to go out of government employment voluntarily, seeking an order of retirement from the Government for enabling him to do so. The exercise of such option by a government servant does not involve any other government servant in the process. So far the Government has been given the power to retire, a government servant who has completed 25 years of service, its exercise may or invariably does involve a number of government servants similarly situated. For example, in the present case, a large group of doctors who attained 25 years of service out of which only the appellant and three others were selected by the Government for early retirement were involved. 

 29. In support of the principal ground urged which relates to the invalidity of section 9(2) of the Act as being violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, the learned counsel for the appellant relied on a number of decisions. To begin with reference was made to the case of Ram Krishna Dalmia vs. Justice Tendolkar, AIR 1958 SC 538, which considered the validity of the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 and the notification issued under section 3 of the Act by the Central Government. Mr. Ahmed drew our attention to the following passage quoted from another judgment of the Indian Supreme Court, namely Budhan vs. State of Bihar, AIR 195 SC 191: 

 "A statute may not make any classification of the person or things for the purpose of applying its provisions but may leave it to the discretion of the Government to select and classify persons or things to whom its provisions are to apply. In determining the question of the validity or otherwise of such a statute the Court will not strike down the law out of hand only because no classification appears on its face or because a discretion is given to the Government to make the selection or classification but will go on to examine and ascertain if the statute has laid down any principle or policy for the guidance of the exercise of discretion by the Government in the matter of the selection or classification After such scrutiny the Court will strike down the statute if it does not lay down any principle or policy for guiding the exercise of discretion by the Government in the matter of selection or classification, on the ground that the statute provides for the delegation of arbitrary and uncontrolled power to the Government so as to enable it to discriminate between per-sons or things similarly situate and that therefore the discrimination is inherent in the statute itself. In such a case the Court will strike down both the law as well as the executive action under such law." 

 31. The learned Counsel submitted that as no principle has been laid down in the Act or section 9 (2) or in the rules therein for selecting or classifying government servants falling within a group for premature retirement and the discretion to do so without such principle had been given to the Government, the principle enunciated as above could be applied to strike down section 9(2) and the impugned order of retirement as ultra vies the Constitution. 

 32. Next, the learned Counsel for the appellant referred to the case of Waris Meah vs. The State, (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 117—PLD 1957 SC 157, which held certain provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (VII of 1947) violative of the equality clauses of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1956 as being discriminatory. The impugned provisions gave power to the Government or the State Bank to determine whether a person offending any provisions of the Act was to be tried under the ordinary law or by an Adjudication Officer or by a Tribunal. Munir C.J. who delivered the judgment of the Court observed that: 

 33. In distinguishing the decision pronounced by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Jibendra Kishore Achhara Chowdhury vs. The Province of East Pakistan. (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 21= PLD 1957 SC 9, Munir, C.J. observed that no analogy could be drawn between the impugned provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulations Act and the provisions of the E. Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, whose constitutionality was challenged in the aforesaid case. The provisions of this Act which were impugned were held to be not unconstitutional as they had intended to eliminate all rent-receiving interests and to create a uniform class of tenants under the Government and that section 3 of the Act gave the power or discretion to acquire simultaneously or from time to time, the interests which were to be terminated. In rejecting the contentions that the Act in question Jibendra Kishor Achharya Chowdhury's case was on the face of it discriminatory, the Supreme Court held that: 

 "Three tribunals with different powers and procedures have been set up. The Act creating them contains no indication as to which class or classes of cases are to go before a Court and which before the Tribunal and the Adjudication Officer and it does not impose upon the Central Government, the obligation or expressly confer on it the power, of making rules with a view to classifying the cases to be tried by each of these tribunals. Nor does it define the principle or policy on which such classification may be made by the Central Government or the State Bank." 

 35. Mr. K.A, Bakr, the learned Attorney General, drew our attention to the passage which I quoted above from Jibendra Kishore's case and asserted that it gave authority for his submission that since the impugned Public Servants (Retirement) Act empowered the Government to  retire any Government servant who had completed 25 years of service, the Act could not be said to be discriminatory on the face of it, The learned Attorney-General however, could not show us how or on what principle a government servant, out of a group of so many other government servants similarly placed like him, can be elected by the Government for retirement under section 9(2) without any discrimination. In Jibendra Kishore's case the acquisition of the interests of rent-receivers was not "piece—meal but wholesale" as was pointed out by the learned Chief Justice No selection was involved. The interests of all rent-receivers throughout the province were to be acquired at one and the same time. 

 "It is clear; therefore that inequality is writ large on the Act and is inherent in the very provisions of the taxing section. It is also clear that there is no attempt at classification in the provisions of the Act. Hence, no more need be said as to what could have been the basis for a valid classification. It is one of those cases where the lack of classification creates inequality. It is, therefore, clearly hit by the prohibition to deny equality before the law contained in Art. 14 of the Constitution. Further more, Sec. 7 of the Act, quoted above, particularly the latter part, which vests the Government with the power wholly or partially to exempt any land from the provisions of the Act, is clearly discriminatory in its effect and, therefore, infringes Art. 14 of the Constitution. The Act does not lay down any principle or policy for the guidance of the exercise of discretion by the Government in respect of the selection contemplated by Section 7." 

 37. In another case decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan namely, East and West Steamship Vs. Pakistan, (1958) 10 DLR (SC) 52=PLD 1958 (SC) 41, constitutionality of the provisions of Section 3 of the Control of Shipping Act (XXVI of 1947 which provides that no ship registered in Pakistan shall be takes to sea from a port or place within or outside Pakistan except under a valid licence granted by a shipping authority was challenged on the ground that it infringed, among others, the equality provisions in the Constitution of Pakistan, 1956. Manir, C.J. delivering the judgment observed that; 

 38. While referring to the reliance of the learned Judges of the High Court Division on the observations made in the case of Matajoy Dobey vs. H.C. Share, AIR 1956 (SC) 44 at p. 48 that "a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory power and that abuse of power is not to be easily assumed where the discretion is vested in Government and not in a minor official", the learned Counsel submitted that the action taken against the appellant was obviously discriminatory, no reason has been offered and no fact has been stated by the Government from which the basis of the action could be discerned. The learned Counsel cited the case of Padfield vs. Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, ALL. E.R. 1968 694, in which the House of Lords had the occasion to consider the limits of the exercise of the discretionary statutory powers by a Minister and the extent of the judicial control over such exercise. 

 39. Facts of this case were that the appellants who were the members of a regional committee of the Milk Marketing Board made a complaint to the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food under section 19 (3) (b) of the Agricultural Marketing Act, 1958, requesting him to refer the complaint to the Committee of Investigation set up under the Act. In declining to refer the matter to the Committee the Minister gave reasons which included that the complaint raised wide issues which he did not consider suitable for investigation and that he had unfettered discretion and that if such complaint was upheld by the committee, a statutory order would have to be given by him to give effect to its recommendations. It was held that where a statute conferred discretion on a Minister to exercise a power but did not expressly limit or define the extent of his discretion, his discretion was nevertheless limited to the extent that it must not be so used as to frustrate the objects of the statute. Further, though the Minister had full or unfettered discretion he should not in exercising it, misdirect himself in law, or take into account irrelevant matters, or omit relevant matters from consideration. As to the extent of judicial control over the exercise of discretionary statutory powers, the Court observed that though the Minister gave no reasons for his decision, whether or not to exercise a discretionary power conferred on him by statute, it would not prevent the Court from reaching a conclusion in a proper case that prerogative order should issue. 

 "It is quite clear from the Act of 1958 in question that the Minister is intended to have some duty in the matter. It is conceded that he must properly consider the complaint. He cannot throw it unread into the waste paper basket, He cannot simply say (albeit honestly) "I think that in general the investigation of complaints has a disruptive effect on the scheme and leads to more trouble than (on balance) it is worth: I shall therefore never refer anything to the Committee of investigation." To allow him to do so would be to give him power to set aside for his period at Minister the obvious intention of Parliament, namely, that an independent committee set up for the purpose should be available to Parliament. This was clearly never intended by the Act of 1958. Nor was it intended that he could silently thwart its intention by failing to carry out its purposes. I do not regard a Minister's failure or refusal to give any reasons as a sufficient exclusion of the Court's surveillance. If all the prima facie reasons seem to point in favour of his taking a certain course to carry out the intentions of Parliament in respect of a power which it has given him in that regard, and he gives no reason whatever for taking a contrary course, the court may infer that he has no good reason and that he is not using the power given by Parliament to carry out its intentions." (p. 714) 

 42. For proper carrying out of the purposes of an Act, discretion is sometimes conferred on the Government or the named Authority, but such discretion is not boundless or without its limits, though they may not appear from the provisions conferring the discretion. Where such limits do not appear from the language employed in the Act, it is claimed that the discretion is unfettered. In answering whether the discretion conferred on the Minister was unrestricted or "unfettered" as was claimed by him, Lord Upjohn observed as follows: 

 43. Referring to the observations of the learned Judges of the High Court Division that the superior Courts of this sub-continent found similar provisions of law empowering the Government to retire a public servant prematurely after attainment of certain age or completion of certain years of qualifying service valid and not violative of the equality clauses in their respective Constitutions and also that they upheld the discretion of the Government in retiring a government servant under such provisions of law, Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submitted that a proper analysis of the decisions of these Courts would reveal that in most of these cases infringement of equality clause was not urged and, secondly, where such infringement had been urged, it was found that there was no such infringement, because, either the expressions "public interest" occurred in the Act itself or similar expressions or grounds existed in the rules made under the relevant laws providing for exercising discretion in prematurely retiring a government servant. If the laws did not provide any principle or guideline for regulating the exercise of discretion by the Government in so retiring a government servant, rules made thereunder provided such a principle or guideline. 

 45. In the State of Bombay vs. Saubhagachand M Doshi, AIR 1957 SC 892, the Government was empowered under Service Rules to retire any Government servant on completion of 25 years of service or 50 years of age without giving any reason. The right to compulsorily retire was, however, not to be exercised except when it is in the public interest necessary to dispense with the further services of a government servant such as on account of inefficiency or dishonesty. In cases in which it was seen that the efficiency of the government servant had suffered and it was not desirable to make formal charges against him on such ground and cases were also there where corruption was being indulged in by a government servant but no specific charges were likely to be proved against him. The power of compulsory retirement could be used. No ground was urged on the violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The order of compulsory retirement was not viewed as removal within the meaning of Article 311 of the Indian Constitution. 

 46. In Shiva Charana vs. State of Mysore. AIR 1965 SC 280, Government was empowered under rule 285 of the Mysore Civil Service Rules to retire compulsorily a government servant in public interest after he completed 25 years of service or attained 50 years of age, though the age of normal superannuation was fixed at 55 years. This power could be exercised if retirement was considered necessary in the public interest, provided also notice was given to the government servant concerned at least 3 months before he was required to retire. Notice, in fact, was issued to the appellant. It was held that the compulsory retirement was not removal under Article 311 and the Service Rules empowering the government to compulsorily retire a government servant did not contravene the equality provisions of the Indian Constitution. 

 47. In Tara Singh vs. the State of Rajas than, AIR 1975 SC 1487, the appellant was retired on completion of 25 years of qualifying service and notice requiring the appellant to retire with effect from the date of the expiry of 3 months from the date of the notice was served upon the appellant. In the notice mention was made that the Government was satisfied that it is in the public interest to dispense with further service of the appellant. After having considered the arguments of the learned Counsel and the cases cited by him in support of his contentions that section 9(2) violated Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, I am of the view that since neither the impugned provisions of the Act nor the rules containing them provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government when it proposes to retire a government servant from amongst a group of government servants similarly situated and holding similar jobs, there invariably exists the scope for arbitrary exercise of such discretion. It was not the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the government cannot have or claim the power to retire a government servant after the completion of 25 years of service, though the age of superannuation has been fixed at 57, but what is of importance and consequence to the government servant concerned who is proposed to be retired on completion of 25 years of service is that the discretion of the relevant authority must be seen to have been exercised on some such principles as are discernible in Fundamental Rule 56, Notes 2, East Bengal Service Rule and Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973. Where such basis has been provided by the enunciation of such principles, whether, under the Act or Rules made under an Act or even in the note to such Rules regarding the retirement of government servants, the concerned authority before exercising its discretion, has to con-form to the principles so provided therein, Such principles may be elaborately stated, as in rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973, but even if the rules made under an Act or note appended to any rules providing retirement on the completion of 25 years merely mention that the service of such government servant who has completed 25 years is not necessary in the interest of public service or in public interest, some basis for classification or selection is discernible. Where such basis has been provided, if the government servant concerned challenges the action of government in retiring him on completion of 25 years what the Government has to do is to show that his retirement was necessary in public interest or in the interest of public service. On the other hand, the provisions of section 9(2) coupled with the omission of such basis in the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1975 leaves scope to the concerned authority to arbitrarily retire a government servant who has completed 25 years of service. Had the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Rules. 1975 provided principles as embodied in Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants ( Retirement) Rules, 1973 which were made under similar provisions of law as in section 9(2) of the Act, no challenge could perhaps have been made as to the constitutionality of the impugned provisions of this section. The existence of such principles as are found in the Rules of 1973 would have provided a complete answer to any such challenge to their constitutionality, in spite of the expression "without assigning any reason" used in section 9(2) of the Act. In such a case the authority concerned would have remained free, so as not to disclose any reason in the retirement order, but if its action in retiring a government servant was challenged as arbitrary as has been done by the appellant in the present case, the authority could have disclosed before the Court the basis of its action,

 83. A government servant's right to continue in service is subject to the pleasure of the President. In English Common Law, a government servant, unless otherwise provided by law, holds office during the pleasure of the Crown. This principle has been recognized in the Constitution of the Republic of Bangladesh. Article 134 provides that except as otherwise provided by the Constitution every person in the service of the Republic shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. The very opening words, namely, "except as otherwise provided by the Constitution" indicate that the "pleasure of the President', doctrine is not absolute. This is subject to other constitutional provisions. Under Article 133 of the Constitution the Parliament has been given the power to regulate by law the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic. It also empowers the President to make rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of such persons until provision in that behalf is made by or under any law. Then Article 135 provides two important exceptions. Firstly, a government servant cannot be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action intended to be taken against him. Secondly, no government servant can be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority.
