All the arguments of the learned Attorney-General advanced on this point practically centered on the authority of the Government provided under the impugned statute that is to say, it is an absolute rights of the government to retire any officer after he has completed 25 years of qualifying service without assigning any reason. He referred to the statement made in the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the government before the High Court Division, to the following effect: 

 86. It has already been pointed out that Act XII of 1974 provides no guideline for the discretion by the authority. The position as stated above lends full support to the arguments of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed that in the absence of any principle or guideline for the exercise of the uncontrolled and unqualified discretion under sub-section (2) of section 9, provided the scope to the authority to pick and choose and to discriminate between government servants similarly placed on completion of 25 years of service in the matter of premature retirement; and such discrimination is inherent in the Act itself. Therefore, sub-section (2) of section 9 is violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 

 90. Sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 merely provides that government may at any time retire from service a public servant who has completed 25 years of service without assigning any reason. Rule, 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules 1975 is completely silent with regard to sub-section (2) of section 9. That the statute provides arbitrary, uncontrolled and unguided discretion, and the government is also fully conscious about that, is apparent from the stand taken in the affidavit-in-opposition. Paragraph 12 of the affidavit reflects the stand of the government. It has been categorically stated therein that "the impugned notification was issued in accordance with law." The statement nakedly reflects the view taken by the government in the matter of exercise of the power provided under sub-section (2) of section 9. It is obvious that the government having given the absolute discretion to retire a public servant, the action taken against the appellant should be presumed to have been taken in accordance with law. It further reflects the stand of the government that the government does not owe even a duty to explain to the Court to justify the impugned notification. 

 "The enactment or the rule might not in terms enact a discriminatory rule of law but might enable an unequal or discriminatory treatment to be accorded to persons or things similarly situated. This would happen when the Legislature vests a discretion in an authority, be it the Government or an administrative official acting either as an executive officer or even in a quasi judicial capacity, by a legislation which does not lay down any policy or disclose any tangible or intangible purpose, thus clothing the authority with unguided and arbitrary power enabling it to discriminate...…..In such circumstances the very provision of the law, which enables or permits the authority to discriminate, offends the guarantee of equal protection afforded by Article 14". 

 93. The learned Attorney-General submitted that it should be presumed that the power conferred has not been abused and the authority has discharged its duties honestly and in accordance with law. The presumption that the official action has been taken in accordance with law, will not satisfy the tests to examine the constitutionality of the law. There is nothing in any part of Act XII of 1974 or for that matter in any of the rules framed thereunder, to help classification of government servants out of a number of government servants similarly placed, to whom the prevision of law may be applied. The presumption that the authority will act in accordance with the rule of law can be sustained only if there is a rule of law to guide the authority. No such principle is discernible from any part of the statute. It has already been pointed out that the statute makes a great departure from the provision as contained in rule 342 of the Bangladesh Service Rules and also from President's Order No. 14 of 1972. Thus it leads me to the irresistible conclusion that sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 offends against Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Article 26 of the Constitution declares such a statute void. Consequently by operation of the Constitution as provided under Article 26, sub-section (2) of sec. 9 being violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, is void. 

 94. Section 4 of Act XII of 1974 provides superannuation of a government servant at 57th year of his age, with proviso... that in case of a physician or teacher the government or authority authorized by the government may extend the service upto the age of sixtieth year. The appellant claimed that he was reasonably expecting to continue for the full term of service, and he would continue to serve for the full term but for the illegal termination of his service by way of retirement under the impugned notification. Let me examine whether premature retirement of a government servant before the age of superannuation violates the guarantee provided under Article 135 of the Constitution. 

 95. The appellant was holding the combined office of the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. An earlier attempt of the Government to separate the post of Professorship from the post of Director was successfully challenged in a Writ Petition being Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. The appellant under the terms of his appointment was entitled to hold the combined office of Director and Professor. In compliance of that declaration the position was restored to the appellant. He was holding the combined office till he was retired by the impugned notification. 

 96. A person appointed substantively in a permanent post in government service has a right to hold the post until he attains the age of superannuation or is compulsorily retired as per terms of the Service Rules read with guarantee provided under the Constitution. Normally, a government servant cannot be removed from his service unless he is found guilty of misconduct, negligence, inefficiency or any other disqualification enumerated under the service rules, in an appropriate proceedings drawn up against him. Premature retirement is per se a punishment, because the government servant is deprived of his right to continue in service until he attains the age of superannuation and he also loses the benefits of service accrued to him. Termination of service before hid superannuation is undoubtedly 'removal' if not termed as 'dismissal'. It is true that a person in the service of the Republic holds office during the pleasure of the President, and the Parliament has been given the power to regulate by law the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic, but Article 135 provides two exceptions, namely, (i) a government servant cannot be dismissed, re-moved and reduced in rank, unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action intended to be taken against him; and (ii) no government servant can be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority. If the two constitutional requirements are complied with, the government servant concerned has no valid grievance to make before the Court of law. However difficulty arises only when a government servant is removed from service, not for misconduct, inefficiency, etc., but by applying provisions in the service rules or law which empowers the government to terminate service of a government servant without assigning any reason. In the instant case, service of the appellant has been terminated without assigning any reason and without giving him any opportunity even to explain his position before retirement. 

 97. The learned Attorney-General sought to justify the action submitting that termination of service of the appellant was brought about otherwise than by way of punishment, He further submitted that since there is no stigma the action cannot be treated as a punishment. According to him, the appellant has no valid grievance to make before a Court of law, because he cannot claim the protection of Article 135 of the Constitution. In support of this contention the learned Attorney General referred to several decisions of the Indian Supreme Court laying down the principle that a government servant whose service is terminated otherwise than by way of punishment, the government servant concerned cannot claim the protection of Article 311(2) of the Constitution of India. The rule of law laid down in these decisions, in the context of the facts of these cases, does not answer the question raised in the instant case and in the background of the facts of this case. It is to be ascertained as to when an order for termination of service is inflicted by way of punishment and when it is not. It has already been stated that a government servant holding a substantive post acquires a right to hold the post until he attains the age of superannuation or is compulsorily retired, as per terms of a contract, express or implied, or a service rule. He can be removed from the post only when the post itself is abolished or he is found guilty of misconduct, negligence, inefficiency or other disqualifications in an appropriate proceeding in accordance with the service rules read with Article 135 of the Constitution. Termination of service of a government servant so appointed must be in accordance with the service rules which in its turn must be consistent with Article 135 of the Constitution. Any law or rule dealing with termination of service by retirement before the age of superannuation must be so framed as to safeguard the protections to the government servant guaranteed under the Constitution, that is, under the Fundamental Rights as well as under Article 135 of the Constitution. In support of this view reference may be made to the judgment in the case of P.L. Dhingra v. Union of India, AIR 1958 SC 36. In this case legality of the order of the General Manager of the Northern Railway reverting the petitioner from the post he was holding to his substantive post was challenged on the ground of the order being violative of Article 311(2) of the Indian Constitution. Some observations made in the judgment may be of some assistance in the present consideration of the impugned order being violative of Article 135. S.R. Das, C.J. delivering the majority judgment, observed as follows: 

 "Shortly put, the principle is that when a servant has right to a post or to a rank either under the terms of the contract of employment, express or implied or under the rules governing the conditions of his service, the termination of the service of such a servant or his reduction to a lower post is by itself and prima facie a punishment, for it operates as a forfeiture of his right to hold that post or that rank and to get the emoluments and other benefits attached thereto...… One test for determining whether the termination of the service of a government servant is by way of punishment is to ascertain whether the servant, but for such termination, had the right to hold the post. If he had a right to the post as in the three cases hereinbefore mentioned, the termination of his service will by itself be a punishment and he will be entitled to the protection of Art. 311. 

 "In short, if the termination of service is found on the right flowing from contract or the service rules then, prima facie, the termination is not a punishment and carries with it no evil consequence and so article 311 is not attracted. But, even if the Government has, by contract or under the rules, the right to terminate the employment without going through the procedure prescribed for inflicting the punishment of dismissal or removal or reduction in rank, the Government may, nevertheless, choose to punish the servant and if the termination of service is sough to be founded on misconduct, negligence, inefficiency or other disqualification, then it is a punishment and the requirements of Article 311 must be complied with". 

 "The use of expression 'terminate' or 'discharge' is not conclusive. In spite of the use of such innocuous expressions, the court has to apply the two tests mentioned above, namely, (1) whether the servant had a right to the post or the rank or (2) whether he has been visited with evil consequences of the kind herein before referred to? If the case satisfies either of the two tests then it must be held the servant has been punished and the termination of his service must be taken as a dismissal or removal from his service or the reversion to his substantive rank must be regarded as a reduction in rank and if the requirements of the rules and article 311, which give protection to government servant, have not been completed with, the termination of the service or the reduction in rank must be held to be wrongful and in violation of the constitutional right of the servant". 

 99. In this connection reference may also be made to a later decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Moti Ram vs. N.E. Frontier Railway, AIR 1964 SC 600. In this case, constitutionality of rule 148(3) of Railway Establishment Code (1951) and rule 149(3) of Railway Establishment Code (1959) were examined with reference to Article 311(2) of the Indian Constitution. In both the rules the Railway Authority has been empowered to terminate the services of Railway Servants described therein after giving them notice for the specified period, or paying them their salary for the said period in lieu of notice. The rules also provide that such notice will not be required in case of dismissal or removal as disciplinary measure after compliance with the provisions of clause (2) of Article 311(2) of the Constitution, retirement on attaining the age of superannuation and termination of service due to mental or physical incapacity. Constitutionality of the Rules was challenged on the ground of infringement of both Article 14 (corresponding to Article 27 of the Constitution of Bangladesh) and Article 311(2) (corresponding to Article 135 of the Constitution of Bangladesh). Both the rules were declared void on the ground of infringing Article 14. While examining the impact of the said rules on Article 311 of the Constitution, Subba Rao, J. after elaborate discussion with reference to the relevant decisions of that Court, particularly, Shyamlal's case AIR 1954 SC 369 and P.L. Dhingra's case AIR 1958 SC 36 found both the rules violative of Article 14 and Article 311(2) of the Constitution. The learned Judge, in the course of his judgment, observed as follows: 

 "The effect of the two rules is the same; the difference is only superficial which lies more in clever drafting than in their content. Take, for instance, the following two rules (i) the Government may terminate the services of a permanent Government servant at any time or after a specified period but before the normal superannuation age, by way of compulsory retirement; and (ii) the Government may terminate the services of a permanent civil servant by giving him 15 days notice. Arbitrariness is writ large on both the rules; both the rules enable the Government to deprive a permanent civil servant of his office without enquiry. Both violate Article 311(2) of the Constitution." 

 "Article 311 is a constitutional protection given to Government servants who have title to office, against arbitrary and summary dismissal. It follows that Government cannot by rule evade the provisions of the said Article. The parties cannot also contract themselves out of the constitutional provisions." 

 The learned Judge following the principle laid down in P.L. Dhingra's case AIR 1958 SC 86 in preference to that accepted in Shyamlal's case AIR 1954 SC 369 observed as under: 

 “Once that principle is accepted the cases dealing with compulsory retirement before the age of superannuation cannot also fall outside the scope of Article 311 of the Constitution. Age of superannuation is common to all permanent civil servants; it depends upon an event that inevitably happens by passage of time, unless the employee dies earlier or resigns from the post. It does not depend on the discretion of the employer or the employee who earns a well-earned rest with or without pensioner benefits for the rest of his life; it has, by custom and by convention, become an inextricable incident of Government service; and it is an incident of a permanent post. Notwithstanding the rule fixing an age of superannuation, a person appointed to such a post acquires title to it. The same cannot be said of a compulsory retirement before the age of superannuation. It is not an incident of the tenure; it does not work automatically it is not conceived in the interest of the employee; it is a mode of terminating his employment at the discretion of the appointing authority. In effect, whatever may be the phraseology used in terminating the services of a Government employee, it is punishment imposed on him, for it not only destroys his title but also inevitably carries with it a stigma. Such a termination is only dismissal or removal within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution." 

 100. In this context reference may also be made to another decision of the Supreme Court of India, wherein constitutionality of the service rule providing retirement of a government servant before the age of superannuation on the completion of 25 years of service was considered. In the case of Tara Singh, etc. vs. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1975 SC 1487 legality of the orders of compulsory retirement passed against the petitioners under Rule 244(2) of the Rajasthan Service Rules was challenged on the ground of being violative of Article 311(2) of the Constitution. A.N. Ray. C.J., delivering the the judgement of the Court, noticed that although with amended service rule the expression "public interest" was omitted but the Note appended to the Rule supplied the omission. The learned Chief Justice in dismissing the petitions observed as follows: 

 "The right to be in public employment in a right to hold it according to rules. The right to hold is defeasible according to rules. The rules speak of compulsory retirement. There is guidance in the rules as to when such compulsory retirement is made. When persons complete 25 years of service and the efficiency of such persons is impaired and yet it is desirable not to bring any charge of inefficiency, or incompetency, the Government passes orders of such compulsory retirement. The Government servant in such a case does not lose the benefits which a Government servant has already earned. These orders of compulsory retirement are made in public interest. This is the safety valve of making such orders so that no arbitrariness or bad faith creeps in." 

 101. Precisely this is the grievance of the appellant that the impugned order of retirement was made without any such consideration. The learned Attorney General has nothing to put up against the case of the appellants on the ground of inefficiency or incompetency. All that the affidavit-in-opposition contains is that there was no malafide in the order, nor it was made with the ulterior motive or collateral or malafide purpose, but the same was issued in accordance with law. A government servant has a right to hold the post to which he has been substantively appointed. He can be removed from the post only in accordance with the Rules or law governing his service and the same must be in conformity with Article 125 of the Constitution. The power of the government to retire a government servant before the age of superannuation is only on the ground of "public interest". That is to say there must be a case that the government servant concerned suffers from inefficiency or incompetency. The safety valve has been provided in all service rules whether framed under the Government of India Act, 1935 or under the Constitutions of 1956, 1962 and 1973; one thing is common in the matter of causing premature retirement, that "the services of the public servant is considered not necessary in the interest of public service." In the instant case Act XII of 1974 does not contain the safety valve; and the affidavits filed by the government also do not put forward any ground that efficiency of the appellant was impaired, and the government considering it not desirable to bring any charge of inefficiency or incompetency passed the order of retirement. It is true that the order does not contain any stigma, but the very fact that the appellant was selected out of a number of persons similarly placed, and consequently he has been deprived not only from continuing in the employment for the remaining period of his term of service but also from some of the service benefits accrued to him, makes out a case of punishment. In effect, whatever may be the phraseology used in terminating the service, it is punishment imposed on him, for it not only destroys his right to the post held by him, but 'also inevitably carries with it a stigma. Such a termination is "removal" within the meaning of Article 135 of the Constitution. Therefore the statute or Rule providing a, mode of terminating service at the discretion of the authority without complying with Article 135 is unconstitutional. 

 102. Compulsory retirement has been classified as one of the major punishments under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976. The power conferred under clause (2) of Rule 342 of the Bangladesh Service Rules is controlled by the specific condition that "this right will not be exercised except when it is in the public interest to dispense with the further services of an officer". 

 103. Section 7 of Act 1974 as amended provides that government servant voluntarily retiring under sub-section (1) of section 9 will be entitled to leave preparatory to retirement but the government servant compulsorily retired under sub-section (2) of section 9 shall not he so entitled. With reference to this amendment it has been submitted by the learned Counsel that compulsory retirement being itself a major punishment entailing loss of service for the remaining period and loss of the service benefits already accrued to the appellant, amounts to "removal" within the meaning of Article 135 of the Constitution, and Article 135 is attracted to the case. In the cases of P.L. Dhingra, AIR 1958 S.C. 36 and Mott Ram, AIR 1964 S.C. 600, amongst others, two tests have been laid down to determine whether termination of service amounted to punishment. First test is to ascertain whether the servant but for such termination had the right to hold the post. The other test is whether he has been visited with evil consequences, in that loss of service benefits accrued to him. In such a case the order of termination if taken without complying with requirements of Article 311(2) (corresponding to Article 135 of our Constitution) must be knocked down as illegal and void. The impugned action having been taken against the appellant without issuing any notice upon him or giving him an opportunity of being heard before taking the impugned action, the impugned notification is violative of Article 135 of the Constitution. It has been mentioned above that the learned Attorney General sought to argue with reference to some decisions of the Supreme Court of India that the action taken against the appellant not being a punishment, Article 135 has no application. In the decisions referred to by him it has been held that compulsory retirement did not amount to removal under. Article 311 of the Indian Constitution (corresponding to Article 135 of the Constitution of Bangladesh). On perusal of the decisions it appears that none of them supports the stand taken by the learned Attorney General in the context of the facts of this case. Ratio desidendi of those decisions is that:— 

 (1) when a government servant whose efficiency is impaired, but against whom it is not desirable to make formal charges on the ground of inefficiency, and 

 104. Age of superannuation is an incident in all permanent services. It depends upon an event that inevitably happens by passage of time, unless the employee dies earlier or resigns from the post. Same is not in the case of premature retirement before the age of superannuation. It is not an incident of the tenure; it does not work automatically It is a mode of terminating the service at the discretion of the appointing authority. The rules or law providing such power must of necessity provide the necessary guidelines or principles, so that the power cannot be exercised in violation of the service guarantees provided under the Constitution. Article 135 provides the constitutional protection to the government servants, who have title to the office, against arbitrary and summary dismissal or removal. From this it can be safely held that the Government or the Legislature cannot by framing a Rule or by enacting a law evade the guarantees provided under the Fundamental Rights and the protections provided under Article 135 of the Constitution. In my opinion the impugned law, that is, sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII bf 1974 giving the discretion to the government without any guideline, to retire a government servant without assigning any reason, on his completing 25 years of service, is unconstitutional, and as such it is void on this ground also. 

 105. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed forcefully argued that the impugned notification is bad in law as the same is vitiated by malice in law. He submitted with reference to the judgment of the High Court Division dated December 6, 1979 in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 declaring the notification dated November 22, 1978 (so far as it related to the appellant), to have been made without lawful authority, that some persons being envious of the incomparable position held by the appellant in the field of medicine, research and publication of books and articles on medical science, took the impugned action, which is not only arbitrary but also mala fide and for collateral purposes. By the notification dated November 22, 1978 a deliberate attempt was made with a view to getting rid of the appellant as Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research knowing fully well that he would not be willing to hold non-practicing post of Director. He submitted that the said notification relieving the appellant of his duties and designation of Medicine having been declared illegal, the authority with mala fide intention took recourse to sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 for directing premature retirement of the appellant from the government service itself. 

 106. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed referred to a list containing names of 34 doctors in the service of the Government of Bangladesh who on the relevant date when action was taken against the appellant, completed 25 years of service but no action was taken against them. Even the appellant's successor as Director of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research, is senior to the appellant by age and service. On this point the learned Attorney-General found it difficult to meet the argument of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed that the appellant was retired under sub-section (2) of sec. 9 of Act XII of 1974 with the ulterior object of defeating the decision given in favour of the appellant in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. All that he could submit was that along with the appellant 3 other doctors were retired. He, however, failed to point out the basis of the consideration which resulted in the retirement of the 3 doctors along with the appellant among a large number of doctors who completed 25 years of service. When the learned Attorney General was asked to point out from the affidavit-in-opposition whether any ground has been stated therein to justify the impugned action, the learned Attorney General candidly conceded that there is nothing in the affidavit-in-opposition to indicate any basis for taking the impugned action. When he was asked whether he was in a position to know the Court from the government files if there was any allegation against the appellant, the learned Attorney General frankly submitted that even government files do not indicate any allegation against the appellant. Thus the learned Attorney General simply left the Court to guess as to what could be the reason for taking the impugned action against the appellant. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed further submitted that the mala fide of government is palpable in this case. The previous notification was declared illegal on December 6, 1979, but within a short time, that is, on June 5, 1980 the impugned action was taken against the appellant, and in support of the action the Government failed to disclose any ground, even. He submitted that in this case malice has been clearly established. Malice in common acceptation means against a person, but in its legal sense it means wrongful act, done intentionally, without just cause for excuse. 

 108. In the instant case the appellant successfully defeated the previous attempt of the Government to convert the combined post of Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research into non-practising post of Director, and consequent upon the judgment of the Court, the position was restored to the appellant and he was allowed to hold the combined post as before. Soon came the impugned action compulsorily retiring the appellant from government service altogether without assigning any reason. Although malice has not been alleged against particular person or persons, but there is no doubt that even in the absence of any such allegation, the facts appearing from the affidavits clearly established a case of malice in law. It is not the case of the respondents that the authority was not aware of the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. It also cannot be presumed that the authorities while taking the action against appellant was not aware of Rule 342 of the Bangladesh Service Rules. It may be mentioned that the learned Attorney General also did not argue that an action as contemplated under sub-section (2) of section 9 could be validly taken excepting on the ground that the services of the public servant is considered not necessary in the interest of public service. 

 109. In view of what has been stated above I hold that sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 is ultra vires the Constitution being violative of Articles 27, 29 and 135 of the Constitution, I further hold that the impugned Notification dated June 5, 1980 issued under the said invalid provision of law causing premature retirement of the appellant from government service is illegal and void. In the result the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs, 

 Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—Neither the Act nor the rules provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government when it proposes to retire a government servant under section 9 (2). In such case the scope for arbitrary exercise of discretion cannot be ruled out, as has happened in this case. In order to circumvent the previous decision of the High Court Division, the respondents issued the impugned notification which clearly makes out a case of malice in law. In this view of the matter, the opinion is that Section 9 (2) is bad and ultra vires and the impugned notification is illegal and has been made without any lawful authority and therefore is of no legal effect. 

 (a) I agree with my learned brother Fazle Munim, J. that the appeal should be allowed and the impugned order of retirement be declared to have been made without lawful authority, but only on the ground that government's power under section 9(2) of the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Act was exercised for a collateral purpose, that is to say, the impugned order of retirement was made to circumvent the High Court Division's order allowing the Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. 

 114. (2) to explain what I have meant by the views given above. I would add the following words: Law relating to retirement on completion of 25 years of service allowing full pensionary benefits has been in force in the sub-continent since November 15, 1919 when rule 4 of the Civil Service Rules was brought in by Resolution No. EA 1054, made by the Government of India with approval of the Secretary of State for India in Council. It reads thus: 

 "Government will have an absolute right to retire any officer after he has completed 25 .years of service, without necessity to give him reasons and without any claim to compensation in addition to pension." 

 This rule was in operation when the Government of India Act, 1919 came into force from December 23, 1919 and by virtue of section 96B (4) of the said Act, this rule was validated and confirmed. Consequently, article 465A of Civil Service Regulations was brought in by an amendment and since then this provision as to premature retirement has been in force although. Note (1) of this new article 465A shows that the government retains "an absolute right" to retire any officer after 25 years of service "without giving any reasons" and "no claim to special compensation" on this account would be entertained. Note (1) did not create any new right, for this right was already there. This Note came by way of a reminder that government always got this absolute right but it gave a caution that this right should not be exercised except when it is necessary in the public interest. This expression "in the public interest" has been considered to be a sufficient safeguard against arbitrary exercise of this power, when fundamental rights including "equality clauses" were guaranteed by the Constitution law relating to premature retirement came under challenge particularly in India. It was contended that Article 465A of Civil Service Regulations was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Indian Constitution, but this contention was althrough rejected and it was held that law relating to retirement after 25 years service with pension does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Indian Supreme Court even observed that this question is not entertainable any more. In Sivcharan vs. State of  Mysore AIR 1965 SC 280 the Indian Supreme Court held ; 

 "In our opinion this contention can no longer be entertained because it is concluded by a long series of decisions of this Court. This Court has made perfectly clear that so far as the question of compulsory retirement is concerned it must be taken to be concluded by several decisions of this Court and that the law in relation to the validity of the rules permitting compulsory premature retirement of government servants must be held to be well settled by these decisions and need not be reopened." 

 115. (3) But what has not been allowed to be reopened in Indian Courts has been opened in our Courts only because the expression "in the public interest" is not there in section 9(2)' of the Public Servants Retirement Act. But what is public interest the government is the sole judge to determine. Again, while the government got absolute right to retire a public servant after 25 years of service, the government servant does not have absolute right to continue in service till he completes 57 years in age. Section 4 of this Act of course provides that a government servant shall retire on completion of 57 years of age, but this section must be read with section 9 which provides that government may retire a government servant after he completes 25 years of service or he may himself opt for the retirement. On harmonious interpretation of different provisions of this Act it appears that section 4 is controlled by section .9 and that a government servant shall have a right to continue in service till completion of 57 years of service if he crosses the hurdle after 25 years of service. It has been observed in the elaborate judgment of may learned brother Fazle Munim, J. that in spite of the omission of the expression "public interest", section 9(2) would have been a valid law had there been a corresponding rule providing a minimum guideline or principle as to how the government's power to retire a person should be exercised. If this is so, the law need not be struck down, and while giving relief to the appellant on the other ground an observation pointing out this defect in the law would serve the purpose. According to established principles of interpretation constitutionality of a law must be presumed. I would leave here reiterating that one of the cardinal principles of interpretation is that a law should be interpreted in such a way that it should be rather saved than destroyed and that the Court should lean in favour of upholding constitutionality of a law. 

 116. (4) As, to the question whether premature retirement is violative of Article 135, excepting a passing reference, this was not pressed by the learned Counsel for the appellant. A government servant is retired with full pension after 25 years service not as a measure of punishment. It does not bear any stigma, nor any imputation is made or allegation is brought against the government servant when thus retired with pension. It cannot be ordered before completion of 25 years service which is fairly a long period for earning pension. There may be many reasons for this kind of retirement, such as loss of efficiency, bad reputation administrative exigencies or some other overriding consideration relating to policy or administration. When the public servant is being rewarded with pension, he need not be informed of the reason in the same way as he is not required to give any reason when he himself opts to retire. Government cannot retain him in service even if his service is still required in "public interest" after 25 years of service. A show cause notice for retirement will result in the starting of a departmental enquiry on specific allegation and if the allegation is proved he will be retired as a punishment, but at the same time rewarded with a pension. If the allegation is proved he will better be dismissed or removed in which case no pension will be required to be paid. In such a case the system of retirement after 25 years of service may be abolished and the age of superannuation itself, may be reduced. The Indian Supreme Court has consistently held that premature retirement is not a punishment and it does not amount to removal, in a number of cases, particularly, Shyamlal vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1954 SC 369, Shivcharan vs. State of Mysore, AIR 1965 SC 280, Bisnunarayan vs. State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1965 SC 967 and Tarashing vs. State of Rajasthan AIR 1975 SC. 1487 I find no reason to take a different view in this case Section 9(2) is not violative of Article 135.
